sentences.text: Beginning in February of 2016, the Firm was named as a defendant in multiple purported antitrust class actions now consolidated into a single proceeding in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York ("SDNY") styled In Re: Interest Rate Swaps Antitrust Litigation.
On February 28, 2024, the parties reached an agreement in principle to settle the class claims.
Beginning in 2011, several individual and putative class actions were filed against the Corporation, BANA, and certain Merrill Lynch entities, as well as other banks on the U.S. Dollar LIBOR panel.

Defendants' motion for summary judgment is pending on all remaining claims, brought by individual plaintiffs and one class of plaintiffs who purchased over-the-counter instruments incorporating LIBOR.

comparisons.peer_topic: Interest Rate Swap Antitrust Litigation Status and Settlement
comparisons.peer_summary: Citigroup and related entities are defendants in consolidated antitrust litigation regarding interest rate swap trading, with the court denying class certification in December 2023 and granting preliminary approval of a settlement in July and October 2024.
comparisons.comparison: Both Morgan Stanley and Citigroup are defendants in the same consolidated industry-wide proceeding, In re: Interest Rate Swaps Antitrust Litigation, pending in the SDNY. Both disclosures highlight the identical procedural milestone of December 15, 2023, where the court denied class certification. Both also report that preliminary approval of a settlement was granted by the court on July 11, 2024. While both reached settlement approval in July 2024, Citigroup's disclosure notes an additional approval in October 2024 (implied by the summary 'July and October'), whereas Morgan Stanley's disclosure only cites the July date. Both filings indicate a similar trajectory from denied class certification to preliminary settlement approval within the 2024 fiscal year.

comparisons.peer_topic: Interest Rate Swap Antitrust Litigation Status and Settlement
comparisons.peer_summary: Goldman Sachs entities are defendants in consolidated interest rate swap antitrust class and individual actions filed between 2015 and 2018. On July 11, 2024, the court preliminarily approved a settlement between the plaintiffs and certain defendants, including the firm, for which the firm has paid its full contribution into escrow, while the individual actions remain pending.
comparisons.comparison: Both Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are defendants in consolidated antitrust actions regarding interest rate swap trading in the SDNY. A key similarity is that both entities saw the court grant preliminary approval of a class action settlement on July 11, 2024. However, a significant difference exists in the scope of litigation and resolution: Goldman Sachs explicitly states that while the class action settlement was approved, the firm has 'paid its full contribution into escrow,' indicating financial resolution for that specific claim. In contrast, Morgan Stanley's disclosure for 2024 only notes the agreement in principle and preliminary approval, without confirming final payment or escrow deposit. Additionally, Goldman Sachs discloses that individual actions (filed by operators of swap execution facilities) remain pending, whereas Morgan Stanley's text focuses primarily on the class claims settlement.

sentences.text: On February 28, 2024, the parties reached an agreement in principle to settle the class claims.
On July 11, 2024, the court granted preliminary approval of the settlement.

Group Inc., GS&Co., GSI, GS Bank USA and Goldman Sachs Financial Markets, L.P. are among the defendants named in a putative antitrust class action relating to the trading of interest rate swaps, filed in November 2015 and consolidated in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

The same Goldman Sachs entities are also among the defendants named in two antitrust actions relating to the trading of interest rate swaps, commenced in April 2016 and June 2018, respectively, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York by three operators of swap execution facilities and certain of their affiliates.

comparisons.peer_summary: The monetary relief class action settled for ~$6.2 billion with $700 million returned to defendants; a separate injunctive class action saw preliminary approval denied in June 2024, while individual actions by opting merchants have mostly settled representing over 70% of sales volume. Ongoing matters include a Swiss EURIBOR investigation and a U.S. Court of Appeals affirmation of a dismissal in an antitrust lawsuit; the Firm has resolved all non-U.S. dollar LIBOR actions and obtained dismissals or moved for summary judgment in remaining U.S. dollar LIBOR cases.
comparisons.comparison: Both Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase disclose antitrust litigation related to interest rate benchmarks in the SDNY. Morgan Stanley's litigation concerns Interest Rate Swaps, where a settlement was preliminarily approved in July 2024. JPMorgan's disclosure for the same item covers multiple matters, including U.S. dollar LIBOR and interchange fees. Regarding LIBOR, JPMorgan notes that while class certification was granted for certain swap/bond claims, an antitrust lawsuit alleging conspiracy to set LIBOR was dismissed in October 2023 and affirmed on appeal in December 2024. Thus, JPMorgan achieved a dismissal/affirmance in 2024, whereas Morgan Stanley achieved a settlement approval in the same year. The topics are related (benchmark antitrust) but involve different benchmarks (Swaps vs. LIBOR) and opposite outcomes (settlement vs. dismissal).

sentences.text: On February 28, 2024, the parties reached an agreement in principle to settle the class claims.
On July 11, 2024, the court granted preliminary approval of the settlement.

In actions related to U.S. dollar LIBOR during the period that it was administered by the BBA, the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York granted class certification of antitrust claims related to bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by the defendants, including the Firm.

In addition, a lawsuit filed by a group of individual plaintiffs asserting antitrust claims, alleging that the Firm and other defendants were engaged in an unlawful agreement to set U.S. dollar LIBOR and conspired to monopolize the market for LIBOR-based consumer loans and credit cards was dismissed in October 2023 and affirmed on appeal by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in December 2024.
